Part 5

Our rule

Parts 3 and 4 built DINO and SelfPatch. This part is about the change this thesis makes to them: a new way to choose, for every patch, which other patches it should agree with and which it should disagree with, and a contrastive loss that acts on those choices. You will see the rule exactly as the code computes it, run it on real tokens, walk its loss and its gradient number by number, follow the three runs as they trained, and read what the frozen decoder and the linear probe measured afterwards.

5.1 The question, and the picture behind it

Assumes: Parts 3 and 4: a student and a teacher, tokens, SelfPatch's 3 × 3 window. Gives: the question of the runs in one sentence, and the picture of islands that the rule aims at.

The question, in the protocol's words: does a patch objective whose positives are the most similar patches anywhere in the crop, and whose negatives are the crop's least similar fifth, change the label-free mask quality, against the released start and the campaign's SelfPatch runs from the same start? Fact

Picture a photograph of a dog and a cat by a door. Cut into a grid of patches, the dog covers many patches, the cat a few others, and the door and the floor the rest. If the model's tokens worked as we hope, every patch of the dog would carry a token close to every other patch of the dog and far from the patches of the cat and the floor. The tokens would form islands of agreement, one island per object, and a decoder could read an object as an island. Toy

The image comes from GLOM, a paper that says it describes no working system: it proposes to represent the parts of an image by islands of identical vectors. This course uses GLOM as a picture, never as a method. Fact

SelfPatch, in Part 4, pulls each patch towards some of its 8 neighbours in its 3 × 3 window, and towards nothing else. Two things are missing for islands. A patch of the dog's ear can only agree with patches right next to it, so agreement creeps across an object one window at a time. And nothing in SelfPatch's loss ever pushes two patches apart: between patches it has attraction only. Fact

On 8 October 2026 the supervisor proposed, instead of SelfPatch's 3 × 3 window, to rank every patch against all other patches of the crop, take the top k as positives and the bottom k as negatives, do the same with a shared threshold for the image level, and change the loss accordingly. Fact

The owner then fixed the run in the chat of the same day: one run, with the row level and the image level combined, positives from the top k of all the patches, negatives from the lowest K per cent, and k fixed for the first run. For the loss the owner asked whether to keep SelfPatch's or to bring in a contrastive loss beside DINO's global loss; the lead recommended a contrastive loss on the tokens in place of SelfPatch's patch term, with DINO's global loss unchanged, and the owner proceeded. Fact

Decision

An anchor's candidates are every other patch of its crop: 195 on a 224-pixel crop and 35 on a 96-pixel crop, wherever they lie.

Why

On the released model only 43.6 % of an anchor's 8 most similar patches lie inside SelfPatch's 3 × 3 window, at a mean grid distance of 2.65, so most of the patches that already agree with an anchor lie outside its window. Fact

Evidence

By chance a candidate falls inside the window 8 times in 195 at 224 pixels; the measured 43.6 % is far above that, so the window holds the closest agreements and misses most of the rest. SelfPatch's own ablation found the opposite for its rule: candidates from all patches scored 47.3 against 57.0 for the 3 × 3 window, a DAVIS label-propagation number of a smaller ViT-Ti/16 pre-trained on COCO. Our rule adds a floor, a threshold, caps and negatives, which that ablation did not have. Fact

What it does to training

The pull now reaches patches of the same object that are far apart in the crop, so agreement can spread across an object in one step instead of creeping from neighbour to neighbour. Toy

If you changed it

Back to the window is SelfPatch's rule. One of run 1's comparators, the row twin of 5.7, is that control: SelfPatch's own term and window rule, trained from the same start with the same images, and section 5.9 reads it beside run 1. Fact

Decision

The contrastive term replaces SelfPatch's patch term; it is not added beside it. DINO's global term stays unchanged.

Why

The lead recommended, and the owner accepted by proceeding, a contrastive term on the tokens in place of SelfPatch's patch term, with DINO's global term unchanged; keeping SelfPatch's patch term beside the new term was left out of scope. Fact

Evidence

The contrastive term puts the positives and the negatives into one formula on the tokens, which is why it was chosen over three pushes that would each have been added beside SelfPatch's pull: a bounded hinge on the prototype overlaps, which the first premise test found nearly idle for the least similar pairs; a direct push on the overlaps, which only re-weights an existing tiny gradient; and a hinge on the token cosines, a separate term beside a pull in another space. The run spec left all three out of scope. Fact

What it does to training

Every patch-level gradient now comes from one formula. SelfPatch's patch head, with its 4,096 prototypes, stays in the model and in every saved file, but the student's forward skips it, so it receives no gradient and AdamW leaves it alone. Fact

If you changed it

Keeping both terms was left out of scope, so no run has tried it. A patch would then be pulled twice, once through the prototypes and once on the tokens, and the reading could not tell which pull moved the decoder. Toy

5.2 The rule, exactly as built

Assumes: 5.1, cosine similarity (Part 1), crops and the teacher (Part 3). Gives: every step and every constant of the rule, the code that computes it, and a worked example on a toy crop.

The rule runs on every crop of every image at every optimiser step. An image gives ten crops: two global crops of 224 pixels, each a grid of 14 × 14 = 196 patches, and eight local crops of 96 pixels, each a grid of 6 × 6 = 36 patches. Every patch of a crop is in turn the anchor, and the rule gives it two sets: its positives and its negatives. Fact

  1. Similarity. Take the teacher's final-block tokens of the crop, scale each to length 1, and compute the cosine of every pair: a table of N × N numbers, the diagonal (a patch with itself) set to minus infinity so that it never counts. No gradient flows through this table. Fact
  2. Two thresholds. Over the crop's N(N − 1) off-diagonal cosines, τhi is the quantile at 1 − k/(N − 1) and τlo the quantile at 0.20: one high and one low cut for the whole crop. Fact
  3. Positives. The anchor's k most similar candidates (k = 8 on a 224-pixel crop, 4 on a 96-pixel crop), united with every candidate at or above τhi; above 24, the 24 most similar are kept. Fact
  4. Negatives. The candidates at or below τlo that are not positives; above 48, the 48 least similar are kept. Fact
  5. The term. For each positive, an InfoNCE term at temperature τ = 0.2 compares the student's token of the anchor with the teacher's tokens of the positive and of all the negatives. Fact
  6. The objective. L = Lglobal + λ Lcon with λ = 1.0; SelfPatch's patch term is not in it. Fact

Each step is one function of cluster/contrastive.py, and the trainer composes them crop by crop. Fact

StepFunctionWhere
the crop's k (8 or 4)k_forcluster/contrastive.py:110
the cosine tableall_pairs_similaritycluster/contrastive.py:124
τhi and τlothresholdscluster/contrastive.py:131
the positives and the cappositive_maskcluster/contrastive.py:139
the negatives and the capnegative_maskcluster/contrastive.py:161
the InfoNCE term of one viewcontrastive_losscluster/contrastive.py:177
the ten views, divided by tencon_termscluster/train.py:652
Lglobal + λ LconContrastiveGlobalLoss.combinecluster/selection.py:675

The cosine table and the two quantiles

sij = cos(ti, tj) for i ≠ j,   τhi = Q1 − k/(N − 1)({sij}),   τlo = Q0.20({sij})
ti
the teacher's final-block token of patch i: 384 numbers, scaled to length 1
sij
one cosine, a number between −1 and 1; all of them form an N by N table
N
the patches of the crop: 196 at 224 pixels, 36 at 96 pixels
k
the crop's k: 8 at 224 pixels, 4 at 96 pixels
Qq
the quantile at level q with linear interpolation, over the N(N − 1) off-diagonal cosines
τhi, τlo
two scalars per crop: the high cut and the low cut

A toy crop of 4 × 4 = 16 patches (a cat, a ball and grass; the lab below draws it) has 16 × 15 = 240 ordered pairs. Sort their cosines from smallest to largest and number them 0 to 239. Toy

With k = 4 the high level is 1 − 4/15 = 0.7333. Its position is 0.7333 × 239 = 175.2667: between the sorted values number 175 and 176, which are 0.5271 and 0.5332, at 0.2667 of the way. So τhi = 0.5271 + 0.2667 × (0.5332 − 0.5271) = 0.5288 (its last digit comes from the unrounded values). On average each anchor has k = 4 partners at or above it. Toy

The low level 0.2 sits at 0.2 × 239 = 47.8: between number 47 and 48, which are −0.0168 and −0.0077, at 0.8 of the way. So τlo = −0.0168 + 0.8 × (−0.0077 + 0.0168) = −0.0096 (the four-decimal values round its last digit). Toy

On the real followed photograph, under run 2's teacher at its end, the 224-pixel crop has 38,220 such cosines; τhi sits at the level 1 − 8/195 = 0.959 and equals 0.8685, and τlo equals −0.3202. Real

None. The table, the thresholds and the sets are computed from the teacher's tokens without gradient: within a step they are fixed numbers that the loss uses, and nothing in the loss can move them. Fact

The thresholds move between steps, because the teacher moves. In run 1 the crops' mean τhi rose from 0.63 to 0.73 and the mean τlo fell from 0.11 to −0.06: the most similar pairs grew more similar and the least similar pairs less similar, as the token space spread. Lab 5E draws both curves. Reading

The positives and the negatives, with their caps

P(i) = cap24( topk(i) ∪ { j ≠ i : sij ≥ τhi } ),   N(i) = cap48( { j ≠ i, j ∉ P(i) : sij ≤ τlo } )
topk(i)
the anchor's k most similar candidates, the row part: a floor, so every anchor has at least k positives
{ sij ≥ τhi }
the image part: every candidate above the crop-wide cut, however many
cap24
keeps the 24 most similar positives; cap48 keeps the 48 least similar negatives
P(i), N(i)
two lists of patch indices per anchor; their sizes vary from anchor to anchor

Anchor 5 of the toy crop (a cat patch) ranks its 15 candidates: 10, 6, 9 and 15 come first, with cosines 0.8122, 0.6783, 0.6281 and 0.5362, then 12 at 0.2974. The row part at k = 4 is {10, 6, 9, 15}. The image part keeps what is at or above τhi = 0.5288: the same four, because 0.5362 is above and 0.2974 below. The union has 4 members, far under the cap of 24. Toy

The negatives are the candidates at or below τlo = −0.0096: patch 8 at −0.0789, 3 at −0.1171, 0 at −0.1213 and 2 at −0.1807, four grass and ball patches, far under the cap of 48. Over the whole toy crop the anchors keep 4 to 7 positives, 4.4375 on average, and 2 to 5 negatives, 3 on average. Toy

On the real crop the followed anchor, patch 34 on the bulldog's nose, keeps 8 positives, all from its top k, because its most similar candidate has cosine 0.8137, below τhi. It has 79 candidates at or below τlo, and the cap keeps the 48 least similar. Real

Across that crop the anchors keep 11.8112 positives and 31.6429 negatives on average; the cap on positives cuts 7 anchors, the cap on negatives 36, 6 anchors have no negative at all, and 747 positive pairs come from the threshold, beyond their anchor's top k. Real

None through the sets themselves: they are chosen without gradient. They decide which terms the loss holds, so they decide where the gradient of 5.4 points. Fact

In run 1 the anchors kept between 8.6 and 8.7 positives and between 20.5 and 21.1 negatives on average from the first step to the last; these means include the eight 96-pixel crops, where k = 4 and an anchor has only 35 candidates. Reading

5.4 The InfoNCE term, walked

Assumes: 5.2, softmax and temperature (Part 1), gradients (Part 1). Gives: the loss of one anchor, number by number, and the force it puts on the student's token.

For an anchor i and one of its positives p, the term asks the student's token of i to be closer to the teacher's token of p than to the teacher's tokens of all of i's negatives at once: it is near zero when the positive wins by a wide margin and grows when any negative comes close. Fact

The InfoNCE term and its gradient

ℓip = −log [ esip/τ / ( esip/τ + Σn∈N(i) esin/τ ) ],   Li = meanp∈P(i) ℓip,   sij = cos(zsi, sg(ztj))
zsi
the student's final-block token of the anchor: 384 numbers; the gradient flows into it
ztj
the teacher's token of patch j of the same crop: 384 numbers
sg( )
stop-gradient: the teacher's tokens are constants for the loss
sip, sin
two cosines: student anchor against the teacher's positive, and against one teacher negative
τ
the temperature, 0.2: dividing by it stretches the cosines before the exponentials
wp, wn
the shares of the denominator: wp = e−ℓip for the positive, and the negatives' shares add up to 1 − wp
ℓip, Li
one scalar per (anchor, positive), and its mean over the anchor's positives

At the start of the toy, the student's tokens equal the teacher's, so the cosines are those of 5.2. Anchor 5 has four negatives. Their es/0.2: patch 2, e−0.1807/0.2 = 0.4052; patch 0, 0.5453; patch 3, 0.5568; patch 8, 0.674. Their sum is 2.1814, the same for every positive of the anchor. Toy

Positive 10: e0.8122/0.2 = 58.0453, the denominator 58.0453 + 2.1814 = 60.2267, its share w = 58.0453 / 60.2267 = 0.9638, and ℓ = −log 0.9638 = 0.0369. Positive 6: 29.7134 / 31.8947 = 0.9316, so ℓ = 0.0708. Positive 9: 23.1153 / 25.2967 = 0.9138, so ℓ = 0.0902. The tail, positive 15: 14.5968 / 16.7782 = 0.87, so ℓ = 0.1393. Toy

L5 = (0.0369 + 0.0708 + 0.0902 + 0.1393) / 4 = 0.0843. At τ = 0.1 it would be 0.0024 and at τ = 0.3 it would be 0.265: a lower temperature makes the negatives' exponentials tiny next to the positive's, so the term shrinks. Toy

A note for checking by hand: the numbers above come from the toy's unrounded cosines, as Lab N computes them, and are rounded only at the end. Redone from the four-decimal cosines printed here, the exponentials and their sums can move in their second to fourth decimal, while every share and the three values of L5 come out the same, and each term the same or one apart in its last digit. Toy

The real followed anchor under run 2 at its end has L = 0.0483 at τ = 0.2; its positives hold 0.9529 of their denominators on average and its negatives 0.0471. At τ = 0.1 its term is 0.0000605 and at τ = 0.3 it is 0.392. Real

The gradient on the student's token is d ℓip / d zsi = (1/τ) [ −(1 − wp) gip + Σn wn gin ], where gij is the gradient of the cosine sij. A step against it pulls the token towards the positive with the weight (1/τ)(1 − wp) and pushes it away from each negative with the weight (1/τ) wn: the pull's weight is the pushes' total. Fact

For the toy tail, the negatives hold 1 − 0.87 = 0.13 of the denominator, split 0.0242, 0.0325, 0.0332 and 0.0402 between patches 2, 0, 3 and 8. The pull towards the tail has the weight 5 × 0.13 = 0.65, and each negative pushes with five times its share, the most alike negative hardest. Toy

The real followed anchor's gradient, computed by PyTorch through the token's normalisation, has length 0.1582: its pull part 0.0987 and its push part 0.1234. Real

In run 2 the contrastive term was 0.7336 at step 1, 0.0372 at step 4,620 and 0.0269 at step 9,240, and the negatives' share of the denominators fell from 0.4976 to 0.0462 and then 0.0326. As the negatives drift away their shares shrink, and so does every pull and push: the term works hardest at the start. Real

In the lab below, the followed anchor's term is rebuilt from the real student and teacher tokens of run 2, step by step for one positive, and checked against the value that PyTorch computed for the bundle. Slide τ and watch the shares and the term; move the positive's cosine with the toy slider; click another anchor of the crop. Real

5.5 Why these choices

Assumes: 5.2 to 5.4. Gives: for each choice of the rule, the reason, the evidence, what it does to training and what changing it would do.

Most of the evidence below comes from the two premise tests: label-free measurements on existing weights, run on a CPU before the run, never a training run. They read the released model on the first 200 images of the image-only COCO v4 manifest. Fact

Several premise numbers use the frozen decoder's regions as a stand-in for objects: a region is a label-free guess, and a positive that shares its anchor's region probably lies on the same object. Fact

Decision

The positives are the anchor's top k united with every candidate at or above the crop-wide quantile τhi.

Why

The row part is a floor, so no anchor is left without positives, while the crop-wide threshold can add more where a crop holds many similar pairs; τhi sits at the quantile 1 − k/(N − 1) so that the pairs above it number k per anchor on average, the same mean as the row part. Fact

Evidence

At 224 pixels the positives that the threshold adds share their anchor's decoder region 93.2 % of the time (91.4 % without background anchors), more often than the row part's 90.0 % (90.1 %); at 96 pixels less often, 61.7 % (55.6 %) against 75.0 % (73.8 %). The image part alone, without the floor, left 33.7 % of the anchors at 224 pixels without any positive in the first premise test. Fact

What it does to training

An anchor inside a large, even region gets many positives and is pulled towards the whole region; an anchor on a boundary keeps its k nearest agreements. The size of each anchor's island adapts to the crop. Toy

If you changed it

The row part alone is the supervisor's first form, a fixed k for every anchor; the image part alone empties anchors. Lab N above has both parts as rules of their own: switch the rule and watch the counts. Toy

Decision

k = 8 on the 224-pixel crops (195 candidates) and k = 4 on the 96-pixel crops (35 candidates).

Why

The owner set k = 8 for the 224-pixel image ("ok proceed with 8"); the lead set k = 4 on the 96-pixel crops, which carry 8 of the 10 views and 80 % of Lcon's weight, because there the premise test's rule moves k: 8 of 35 is 23 % of the row, and the 8th positive's mean cosine is 0.41 against 0.55 for the 4th. Fact

Evidence

The k curve of the second premise test: at 224 pixels the 8th positive shares its anchor's region for 87.1 % of the anchors against 90.0 % for the 4th, within the rule's 10 points, so k stays 8; at 96 pixels 63.5 % against 76.8 %, 13.32 points lower, so the criterion moves k. Before k was set the owner was shown that 4 of 195 candidates is a 2 per cent selection against SelfPatch's 50 per cent. Fact

What it does to training

On the small crops each anchor pulls towards fewer, surer partners, so the pull on the eight local views rests on patches that share the anchor's region more often. Toy

If you changed it

With k = 8 on the 96-pixel crops, almost a quarter of each row would be a positive and more of them would cross into other regions. The protocol allowed that setting by one flag; it was not run. Fact

Decision

A count for the positives (the top k of all the patches) and a percentage for the negatives (the last K per cent of the crop's pairs).

Why

The owner's own words fix the two forms: "top k of all patch" for the positives and "last K percentile" for the negatives. Fact

Evidence

A percentage gives a crop-wide cut, so the number of negatives varies by anchor: on the released model's 224-pixel views the bottom 20 per cent gave 30.6 negatives per anchor (median 29.0), while 0.22 % of the anchors had none. Fact

What it does to training

Every anchor pulls towards its own k most similar partners at least. The negatives come from one cut for the whole crop, its own 0.20 quantile, so every crop offers about a fifth of its pairs as candidates whatever it shows, and inside a crop they fall unevenly: an anchor unlike most of the crop, such as a patch of a small object on a large background, meets many negatives, and an anchor of the dominant region meets few. Toy

If you changed it

A count of negatives (the bottom k of each row) would give every anchor the same number, including anchors whose least similar patches are still fairly similar; the supervisor's first proposal had that form. Fact

Decision

The negatives come from the bottom 20 per cent of the crop's pairs.

Why

Negatives from the bottom 10, 20 or 30 per cent all share their anchor's decoder region for about 16 to 17 % of the pairs at 224 pixels, against 38.0 % for any candidate, while the bottom 20 per cent gives about 31 negatives per anchor. Fact

Evidence

Bottom 10 %: 17.0 negatives per anchor, 16.2 % in the anchor's region; bottom 20 %: 30.6 per anchor, 16.6 %; bottom 30 %: 40.8 per anchor, 16.9 %. The run spec had expected about 39 at 224 pixels and 7 at 96 pixels. Fact

What it does to training

Each push acts on a patch that most likely belongs to another region, and there are enough of them for a crop-wide push without crowding the denominator. Toy

If you changed it

A smaller share gives fewer, surer negatives and a weaker push; a larger share gives more negatives with about the same purity. Slide the percentage in Lab 5A to see the counts change. Toy

Decision

At most 24 positives (the most similar) and 48 negatives (the least similar) per anchor.

Why

The run spec and the protocol fix the caps at 24 and 48 without stating a reason; the second premise test measured what they cut on the released model's 224-pixel views. Fact

Evidence

On the released model's 224-pixel views the cap at 24 cut the positives of 7.2 % of the anchors, and the cap at 48 cut the negatives of 22.6 % of them. Fact

What it does to training

Every anchor weighs the same in the loss, whatever its number of positives: its term Li is the mean over its own positives, and a view's term is the mean of Li over the view's anchors. The cap on positives keeps an anchor's 24 most similar partners, so the pull of an anchor in a large even region rests on its closest agreements. The cap on negatives keeps the 48 least similar candidates and drops the others, the hardest negatives, those nearest τlo. Fact

If you changed it

Without the cap on negatives, the anchors it cuts would keep their hardest negatives, which would hold the largest shares of their denominators, so those anchors would push harder. Without the cap on positives, a large-region anchor's pull would spread over every partner above τhi, each with a smaller weight. Slide both caps in Lab 5A and read the cuts. Toy

Decision

A patch is a positive or a negative of an anchor, never both.

Why

The negative mask leaves out every positive of the anchor, so the two sets never overlap. Fact

Evidence

Only an anchor whose k most similar patches already lie at or below τlo, an outlier unlike the rest of its crop, can meet a patch that qualifies for both sets; the rule keeps it as a positive, because negative_mask takes the positive mask as an argument. Fact

What it does to training

No token is pulled towards and pushed away from the same partner in one term. Toy

If you changed it

A patch in both sets would add a pull and a push on the same direction that cancel in part, and waste the term. Toy

Decision

An InfoNCE term per positive, against all the anchor's negatives at once; neither SelfPatch's prototype cross-entropy nor the pushes that were considered first.

Why

The student's token must be closer to its positive than to all its negatives at once: the term is near zero when the positive wins by a wide margin and grows when any negative comes close. Fact

Evidence

SelfPatch's loss only pulls: no term lowers the agreement of any pair. Of the three pushes considered first, the bounded hinge would be idle for bottom-k negatives by construction, the direct push only re-weights an existing tiny gradient, and a hinge on the tokens sits beside a pull in another space. In neighbour embeddings, a related family of methods, attraction produces continua and repulsion produces discrete clusters, as our report cites from Böhm, Berens and Kobak. SelfPatch's authors tried negatives from other images' global representations with MoBY, a contrastive method, and scored 58.9 with them against 58.4 without, a DAVIS label-propagation number; they found negatives not required and expected that a more elaborate design of negatives might help. Fact

What it does to training

One formula carries both forces, and their weights are the denominator shares: an easy negative pushes little, a close one pushes hard, and the positive pulls with the pushes' total. Fact

If you changed it

SelfPatch's cross-entropy alone would return to attraction only. Lab N above still offers the dropped pushes beside the pull, under its objective switch. Toy

Decision

The temperature of the term is τ = 0.2.

Why

The negatives' share of the denominator, 1 − e−ℓ, is the factor that scales an anchor's gradient, so the criterion asked for a temperature at which the negatives still carry at least 0.3 of it. Fact

Evidence

On one draw of the trainer's crops, with k = 8 on every crop, the released model's negatives held 0.075, 0.394 and 0.609 of the denominator at τ = 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3, so 0.2 is the smallest temperature that meets the criterion. The decided setting, k = 8 on the global crops and 4 on the local ones, was not measured before the run. With k = 4 on every crop the pooled share was already 0.333 at τ = 0.2, and the decided setting can only raise it, because an anchor's positives at k = 8 contain those at k = 4, so τ = 0.2 still meets the criterion; on the local crops alone the share was 0.243, which by itself would ask for τ = 0.3. At the start of run 1 the telemetry read 0.408. Fact

What it does to training

The temperature sets the weight of every pull and push. The pull towards a positive weighs (1/τ)(1 − wp), the negatives' share divided by τ: on the same draw of crops that weight averaged 0.75 at τ = 0.1, 1.97 at 0.2 and 2.03 at 0.3, so at 0.1 the term would have pulled and pushed less than half as hard as at 0.2. Fact

If you changed it

Slide τ in Lab 5B: a lower value gives the positive a larger share of its denominator and the negatives smaller ones, so the term shrinks; a higher value spreads the denominator more evenly over the negatives. A second run was to change one value such as τ if the negatives went inert. Fact

Decision

The contrastive term enters the objective with the weight λ = 1.

Why

λ is 1 because the new term is the point of the run, and both terms are logged separately, so a second run could lower λ if the global features degraded. Fact

Evidence

In run 1 the global term kept falling while the contrastive term acted, to 0.76 of its epoch-0 mean by epoch 20, so the push did not fight DINO's term; the stop rule at 1.2 times that mean never came near. Reading

What it does to training

One unit of the contrastive term weighs as much as one unit of the global term in the gradient on the backbone. Toy

If you changed it

A smaller λ would protect the global term at the price of a weaker push; the stop rule on the global loss existed to call for that. Fact

Decision

Every positive and every negative comes from the anchor's own crop: no memory bank, no other image's patches.

Why

Every positive and negative comes from the anchor's own crop, and the batch scope and hard-negative mining were left out of scope. Fact

Evidence

No run of this study drew negatives from other images. The nearest evidence is SelfPatch's own: with MoBY, negatives from other images' global representations scored 58.9 against 58.4 without them, a DAVIS label-propagation number, and its authors found negatives not required. Fact

What it does to training

The push separates a crop's least similar patches from each other, which is what a decoder reads in one picture; it says nothing about how two pictures differ, which the global term already handles. Toy

If you changed it

Negatives from other images would mostly be far easier and hold tiny shares, and they would differ from the anchor for reasons the decoder never sees; no run has tried it. Toy

Decision

The positives and negatives are chosen on the teacher's tokens without gradient; the loss acts on the student's tokens.

Why

The selection must not be moved by the gradient it creates, as in SelfPatch's official rule. Fact

Evidence

The gradient flows through the student's normalisation into every block of the student backbone, while the teacher's tokens are detached, so the teacher moves only by its moving average. Fact

What it does to training

The targets of a step are fixed before the step, and they change slowly because the teacher is an average of the student's past. Toy

If you changed it

With the student choosing its own partners, every step would also move the partners it chooses, and the loss could drift towards partners that are easy for itself. Toy

Decision

DINO's global term stays, as the trainer computes it: 65,536 prototypes, 18 crop pairs, teacher at 0.04, student at 0.1.

Why

The owner's question offered a contrastive loss combined with DINO's global loss, the lead recommended that design with the global loss unchanged, and the owner proceeded. Fact

Evidence

SelfPatch's aggregation head stays in the global term, because SelfPatch's class token is the aggregation head's own class token attending over the patch tokens; what leaves the loss is the 4,096-prototype patch term. Fact

What it does to training

The global term keeps the image-level summary of the crops in agreement, as in DINO, while the new term works on the patch tokens. Toy

If you changed it

Without the global term nothing would tie the crops of one image together at the image level; the stop rule on the global loss watches that it does not degrade. Toy

Before the run the second premise test also measured the combined rule at k = 8 on the released model: on the 224-pixel views 11.1 positives per anchor (median 8.0), 28.2 % of them from the threshold, the cap at 24 cutting 7.2 % of the anchors; on one draw of the trainer's crops 10.6 positives per anchor, 24.3 % from the threshold. Its verdict set τ = 0.2 and left k to the lead, who decided it before the protocol was committed. Fact

5.6 The projection head of run 3

Assumes: 5.4, a linear layer and GELU (Part 1). Gives: what run 3 changed, and why a head changes the gradient that reaches the backbone.

Run 3 starts where run 1 started and changes one knob: the space of the contrastive term, which moves into a projection head's outputs. Fact

The head is a Linear layer from 384 to 1,024 values with a bias, the exact GELU, and a Linear layer from 1,024 to 256 with a bias, applied to each token alone with no normalisation layer; its outputs are scaled to length 1 before the cosine. Fact

The positives, the negatives, both thresholds, k and the caps are still chosen from the teacher's raw final-block tokens, so the premise calibration and the rule's telemetry keep their meaning; only the term's similarities move into the head's space. Fact

The head moves the term's similarities into a token-wise MLP's space, as SimCLR applies its loss and DenseCL, Leopart and CrIBo their local terms, so that the push shapes the backbone through the head. Fact

What the head costs: two more modules to train and to carry, which add 10.5 MB to run 3's final envelope, the file in which a run saves its state, and a term whose negatives' share and margin are measured in the head's space, so they are not like for like with run 1's. Reading

The projection head

h(z) = W2 GELU(W1 z + b1) + b2,   sij = cos(hs(zsi), sg(ht(ztj)))
z
one final-block token: 384 numbers
W1, b1
a matrix of 1,024 by 384 and a bias of 1,024
GELU
the bend x Φ(x), with Φ the normal distribution's cumulative function
W2, b2
a matrix of 256 by 1,024 and a bias of 256
hs, ht
the student's head, trained, and the teacher's head, its moving average
sij
the term's cosine, now between two 256-value outputs

A toy head from 2 numbers to 3 and back to 2. Take z = (1, 2), W1 with rows (1, 0), (0, 1) and (1, −1), no biases: W1 z = (1, 2, −1). Toy

GELU bends each number: GELU(1) = 0.8413, GELU(2) = 1.9545 and GELU(−1) = −0.1587, so large positive numbers pass almost unchanged and negative ones shrink towards 0. With W2 rows (1, 0, 1) and (0, 1, 1): h = (0.8413 − 0.1587, 1.9545 − 0.1587) = (0.6827, 1.7958), of length 1.9212, which scales to (0.3553, 0.9347). Toy

The term's gradient on h travels back through the head before it reaches the token: through W2, then the GELU's slopes, then W1. The slopes at 1, 2 and −1 are 1.0833, 1.0852 and −0.0833. Toy

Push the toy head's first output by 1 and nothing else: W2 sends 1 to the first and the third hidden numbers, the slopes turn them into 1.0833 and −0.0833, and W1 turns those into (1.0833 − 0.0833, 0.0833) = (1, 0.0833) on z. A push on the head's output reaches the token reshaped: the head decides which of the token's numbers move, and by how much. Toy

Run 3's contrastive term, measured in the head's space, was 0.6444 at step 1 and 0.0538 at step 9,240; it is not like for like with run 1's term, which is measured on the raw tokens. Real

The projection head

Why does a loss in the head's space change the gradient that reaches the backbone?

Toy Real

What you are looking at: run 3's real teacher tokens of the followed photograph at its last epoch, the anchor's sets chosen on those raw tokens with the run's rule, and a head of the real shape. The flow shows the anchor's token at each stage of the head, the bars compare each partner's cosine on the raw tokens and in the head's space, and the readout compares the gradient that reaches the token's 384 numbers on the two paths.

Real model versus this toy: the head is a toy: fresh random weights of the real shape, drawn as a new Linear layer is drawn, because the bundle does not hold run 3's trained head. The student's tokens are taken equal to the teacher's, as at the start of a run. The real run trains its head with the heads' learning rate, and the teacher's head follows by the moving average.

Decision

Run 3 computes the term in a projection head's space: 384 to 1,024, GELU, 1,024 to 256, length 1. The selection stays on the raw tokens.

Why

The head moves the term's similarities into a token-wise MLP's space, as SimCLR applies its loss and DenseCL, Leopart and CrIBo their local terms, so that the push shapes the backbone through the head. Fact

Evidence

Routing the term through the head kept the decoder's primary endpoint, +0.38 [−0.03, +0.78] points over the start (a difference with its 95 % interval in brackets, read as 5.9 explains), and removed run 1's secondary signature, while the linear probe still rose 1.51 mIoU points over the start, level with run 1. One seed. Reading

What it does to training

The head absorbs part of the push: the backbone receives the term reshaped by the head's two layers, so the tokens the decoder reads move less in the term's own directions. Toy

If you changed it

Without the head the push moves the raw tokens directly, which is run 1; section 5.9 reads the two side by side. Fact

5.7 The three runs, and the training in numbers

Assumes: 5.2, the recipe of Part 3. Gives: what each run tests, what it is compared with, and every number of its schedule.

Each further run changes one value against run 1, so that a difference has one cause. Fact

RunStarts fromChangesLaunchedCompleted
run 1the released DINO+SelfPatch checkpointthe rule replaces SelfPatch's patch term2026-10-09 15:23:36 UTC2026-10-10 01:16:28 UTC
run 2the converted DINO ViT-S/16, fresh SelfPatch headsthe start2026-10-10 08:06:49 UTC2026-10-10 17:57:55 UTC
run 3the released checkpoint, as run 1the term in a projection head's space2026-10-10 17:59:41 UTC2026-10-11 04:02:00 UTC

Each run completed its 9,240 steps with none skipped; run 1 trained for 35,521.3 seconds, run 2 for 35,435 and run 3 for 36,088, on one card. Reading

A run draws everything random from one number, its seed: the order in which the images come in each epoch, the crops of every image, the random numbers of every step and, from the DINO start, the first weights of the fresh heads. Two runs with the same seed see the same images in the same order with the same crops; a run with another seed sees other draws. Fact

Besides the starts themselves, two kinds of comparators already existed on disk. The two LC0 twins, named after LC0, the training recipe that they and all three runs share (its numbers are listed below), trained SelfPatch's own patch term from run 1's start, one with SelfPatch's row rule and one with the pooled image rule, with the same seed, initial state, image order, crops and per-step random seeds as run 1, so the contrasts with them are paired by construction. Fact

The pilot is the comparator of run 2 from the same DINO start: DINO trained with SelfPatch's window term under LC0 for 20 epochs, which had spent 0.56 points of the primary endpoint. Fact

The training, in numbers, for all three runs: Fact

  • all 118,287 COCO train2017 images, images only, in batches of 256: 462 optimiser steps per epoch, the last 15 images of each epoch's order dropped;
  • 20 epochs, so 9,240 steps; ten crops per image (2 × 224 + 8 × 96), so 174,080 anchors per step;
  • the heads' learning rate peaks at 1e-4 and ends at 1e-6, the backbone's peaks at 1e-5 and ends at 1e-7, after a linear warm-up of 10 epochs and then a cosine;
  • the backbone is frozen in epoch 0 (steps 1 to 462), so step 463 is the first in which the term can move it; the last layer of each head is held fixed in epoch 0 too;
  • weight decay from 0.04 to 0.4 on a cosine; teacher momentum from 0.9995 to 1; the global term's teacher temperature 0.04 and student temperature 0.1; centre momentum 0.9; each gradient tensor clipped to 3.0; bf16 mixed precision, in which the backbones and the global heads compute with 16-bit numbers while the rule and the term are computed with 32-bit ones;
  • pair 1 of the campaign's paired initial states, seed 906; an envelope every 5 epochs, and the final one, ckpt_epoch020.pt, is the object of the run: no checkpoint is chosen by any score.

The protocol laid the batch out as two cards with four micro-batches of 32 images each; the runs were executed on one card, card 6, with eight micro-batches of 32 images per step, a declared deviation that keeps the global batch at 256. Fact

The total loss with λ

L = Lglobal + λ Lcon,   Lcon = (1/10) Σv meani in view v Li, the sum over the ten views,   λ = 1
Lglobal
DINO's global term: a scalar, the cross-entropy between the teacher's and the student's class outputs over 18 crop pairs
Li
one anchor's term from 5.4, a scalar
v
one of the image's ten views: 196 anchors in a global view, 36 in a local view
λ
the weight of the contrastive term, 1

Toy: if the two global views had terms 0.5 and 0.3 and each of the eight local views 0.4, then Lcon = (0.5 + 0.3 + 8 × 0.4) / 10 = (0.8 + 3.2) / 10 = 0.4, and with a global term of 3.9 the total is 3.9 + 1 × 0.4 = 4.3. With λ = 0.5 it would be 3.9 + 0.2 = 4.1. Toy

At step 1 of run 1 the progress line held a global term of 4.2292 and a contrastive term of 0.4685, so a total of 4.2292 + 0.4685 = 4.6977. Real

The gradient of the total is the gradient of the global term plus λ times the gradient of the contrastive term: both flow into the same backbone, and λ sets their exchange rate. Dividing by the ten views keeps the term's size independent of how many crops an image has, as SelfPatch's patch term divides by the number of views. Fact

In run 1 the contrastive term fell from 0.47 to 0.11 and the negatives' share from 0.41 to 0.11 while the global term kept falling, so the push acted on the token space without fighting DINO's term. Reading

One AdamW step

θ ← θ − η λwd θ;   m ← β1 m + (1 − β1) g;   v ← β2 v + (1 − β2) g2;   θ ← θ − η m̂ / (√v̂ + ε), m̂ = m / (1 − β1t), v̂ = v / (1 − β2t)
θ
one weight of the network (each weight has its own m and v)
g
the weight's gradient at this step, after clipping
η
the learning rate of the step: the backbone's or the heads' schedule
λwd
the weight decay of the step, from 0.04 to 0.4
m, v
running averages of the gradient and of its square; β1 = 0.9 and β2 = 0.999 keep that much of the old value
ε
1e-8, added so that the division never blows up
t
the step number, which corrects m and v for their start at zero

Toy: a weight θ = 0.5 at step 1, gradient g = 0.2, learning rate 0.01, decay 0.04. The decay first takes 0.01 × 0.04 × 0.5 = 0.0002, so θ = 0.4998. Then m = 0.1 × 0.2 = 0.02 and v = 0.001 × 0.04 = 0.00004; corrected, m̂ = 0.02 / 0.1 = 0.2 and v̂ = 0.00004 / 0.001 = 0.04, whose square root is 0.2. The step is 0.01 × 0.2 / 0.2 = 0.01, so θ = 0.4898. Toy

The first step moves the weight by the learning rate, whatever the gradient's size: a gradient a hundred times smaller gives the same 0.01. AdamW reads a gradient's direction and its consistency over steps more than its size. Toy

This is the step itself: it turns the gradients of the loss into a change of every weight. At each step AdamW first shrinks a decayed weight by the learning rate times the decay rate times the weight, then updates m and v, scales both up to make up for their start at zero, which gives m̂ and v̂, and subtracts the learning rate times m̂ / (√v̂ + ε) from the weight. Fact

The schedules of run 1: the backbone's learning rate was 0 at step 1, where its warm-up starts, 1e-06 at step 463, 1e-05 at step 4,620, the warm-up's peak, and 1e-07 at step 9,240; the weight decay was 0.04, 0.0422, 0.2199 and 0.4 at the same steps. Lab 5E draws them. Real

Decision

Run 1 starts from the released DINO+SelfPatch checkpoint; run 2 from the converted DINO ViT-S/16 with fresh SelfPatch heads.

Why

Run 1 starts where the campaign's two LC0 runs of pair 1 started, so its contrasts with them are paired; run 2 changes one knob, the start, to the start of the campaign's pilot. Fact

Evidence

At step 50 run 2's τhi was 0.50 against run 1's 0.64 and its negatives' share 0.49 against 0.41, because DINO's tokens are less alike within a crop than the released SelfPatch model's. Run 2's loss at step 1 was 11.274 against run 1's 4.698, because its SelfPatch heads start fresh. Reading

What it does to training

The two starts give the rule different raw material: from DINO the rule meets a more varied token space and a stronger push at the start. Toy

If you changed it

No run has tried the rule from a scratch start; the project's earlier full-data scratch runs, with no pretrained start, stayed near the decoder's floor. Fact

Decision

20 epochs of 462 steps per run.

Why

Each run trains for 20 epochs of 462 steps, the length of the campaign's LC0 runs it is paired with. Fact

Evidence

On 29 September 2026 the owner confirmed that the 50-epoch branch is dropped: every pilot and campaign run is 20 epochs. A run took about ten hours on one card. Fact

What it does to training

The teacher keeps about a tenth of its step-0 weights after 20 epochs, so most of the run's selection is made by a teacher that training has moved. Fact

If you changed it

Longer runs would let the teacher drift further from its start; no run has tried it, and the pairing with the twins would be lost. Toy

Decision

Recipe LC0: the heads' learning rate peaks at 1e-4, the backbone's at 1e-5, after a 10-epoch warm-up, with the backbone frozen in epoch 0.

Why

Every DINO-initialised dense post-training success the report found moved the backbone in small steps, Leopart and NeCo among them (heads 1e-4, backbone 1e-5); random heads distort pretrained features while they are being fitted, and fitting the head first helps. Fact

Evidence

The campaign's earlier recipe R moved everything at a peak of 5e-4 and was far outside that class. Under LC0 the contrastive term is computed and logged from step 1; in runs 1 and 2 it reaches the backbone only, so it moves nothing before step 463, while run 3's term also trains the projection head during epoch 0, since the freeze discards the backbone's gradients only. Fact

What it does to training

The heads settle first; afterwards the backbone moves a tenth as fast as the heads, so the pretrained token space bends instead of being rewritten. Toy

If you changed it

A larger backbone rate would move the tokens faster and could undo what the start knew; an earlier project run degraded even at a small rate under other confounds. Fact

Decision

A global batch of 256 images per optimiser step.

Why

Every optimiser step uses a global batch of 256 images, as the campaign's recipe and its LC0 runs did. Fact

Evidence

Two 16 GB cards hold neither 128 nor 64 ten-crop images each, so the batch is reached by accumulation; the runs used one card with eight micro-batches of 32 images. DINO's supplement found that small batches work almost as well when the learning rate is scaled with the batch. Fact

What it does to training

The rule and the term work per crop, so the batch size changes how many crops average into one step, never the sets of a crop. Toy

If you changed it

A smaller batch would make each step noisier and break the pairing with the twins. Toy

Decision

Early looks at epochs 5 and 10, and three stop rules read from the telemetry.

Why

The early looks at epochs 5 and 10 were extra validation reads for one decision, continue or stop, and never chose a checkpoint, which stays the final envelope. Fact

Evidence

The stop rules: the negatives' share below 0.02 over an epoch (the negatives are inert), the global loss above 1.2 times its epoch-0 mean (the global features degrade), any non-finite value. They are read from the telemetry and reported, never applied live. Runs 1 and 2 continued at both looks; run 3's looks were not made because the VPN link dropped. Fact

What it does to training

Nothing: a look reads a copy of an envelope and changes no weight. Fact

If you changed it

Choosing a checkpoint by its score would turn the validation panel into a tuning set; the protocol forbids it. Fact

Decision

One seed per run first; second seeds for the two strongest pairs now.

Why

The first runs were one seed each, read descriptively, and a second seed was out of scope until the second seed pair's amendment of 12 October 2026. Fact

Evidence

With one seed the interval of a reading (5.9) holds image sampling only; with two seeds the thesis can say that a reading repeats in both seeds or in one of two, and no more than that. Fact

What it does to training

A new seed gives different crops and different random draws, so a reading that repeats is less likely to be luck. Toy

If you changed it

Many seeds would allow a verdict of different or equivalent, whose rules 5.9 gives; the compute of the deadline allows two. Toy

Decision

Every run is read against comparators trained from the same start: the LC0 twins for runs 1 and 3, the pilot for run 2.

Why

Run 1 shares the seed, the initial state, the batch order, the crops and the seeds of every step's random draws with the campaign's two LC0 runs of pair 1, so its contrasts with them are paired by construction. Fact

Evidence

Runs 1, 2 and 3 saw the same images in the same order: their presentation hashes, fingerprints of the batches that every step drew, are equal, and equal to the twins'. The pilot is DINO trained with SelfPatch's window term under LC0 for 20 epochs from run 2's start. Reading

What it does to training

Nothing for the run itself; for the reading, a paired contrast cancels everything the two runs share, so what is left is the objective. Toy

If you changed it

Against the start alone, a change could come from 20 epochs of any training; the twins and the pilot separate the rule from training as such. Toy

5.8 How the model trains itself: the real telemetry

Assumes: 5.4 and 5.7. Gives: how to read every curve of a progress line, on the real numbers of the three runs.

The trainer writes one progress line per optimiser step with the step, the epoch, the losses, the learning rates, the weight decay, the teacher momentum and diagnostics; the contrastive path adds 14 fields, the term and 13 statistics of the rule. Fact

Read the curves of run 2 from left to right. At step 1 the total loss was 11.2743, the global term 10.5406 and the contrastive term 0.7336, and the negatives held 0.4976 of the denominators. By step 4,620 the term was 0.0372 and the share 0.0462; at step 9,240 the term was 0.0269, the share 0.0326 and the margin between a positive and the closest negative 1.2792. Real

Run 2's negatives' share fell fast at first, each epoch keeping about 75 % of the last, then about 87 %, and it sat near 0.03 for the last five epochs, above the stop line of 0.02. Reading

What the shapes mean. The term and the share fall together, because once the negatives are far their exponentials are tiny and the pulls and pushes weaken. The margin rises as positives and negatives move apart. τlo falls as the least similar pairs grow less similar and τhi rises as the most similar pairs grow more similar: the crop's thresholds move as the token space spreads. In run 1, τhi went from 0.63 to 0.73 and τlo from 0.11 to −0.06. Reading

How the model trains itself

What do the real training curves of the three runs show, step by step?

Real

What you are looking at: the progress lines of runs 1, 2 and 3, sampled at the first step, every tenth step and the first step of every epoch, for the field you choose. The shaded band is epoch 0, when the backbone is frozen; dashed lines mark a stop rule where the field has one. The scrubber reads every chosen run at one step, and the list under the chart says what each field measures. Run 3's term, share and margin are measured in its head's space.

5.9 What the readings showed

Assumes: 5.7 and its seed; the endpoints are explained in Part 6 and, one line each, in Lab 5G below. Gives: how to read a contrast and its interval, the decoder and probe numbers of every checkpoint, and what they do and do not say.

Each run's final envelope was read in one evaluation beside its comparators, by the frozen decoder on the COCO v4 validation panel: 1,000 images, 988 of them defined because 12 hold no retained truth object. A reading is a checkpoint's score on the panel, for most endpoints its mean over the defined images. A paired contrast is the mean, over the same images, of one checkpoint's value minus another's, written as that difference with its 95 % image-bootstrap interval in brackets. Fact

The interval asks how much the contrast could change if the panel had held other images of the same kind. The evaluator draws the panel's 1,000 images again at random with replacement, so that some come twice and some not at all, recomputes the contrast over the defined images drawn, and repeats this 2,000 times (500 times for AP100, the decoder's average precision); the 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles of the results, which hold the middle 95 per cent between them, are the interval's ends. Fact

A toy panel of four images, on which checkpoint b scores 1, −1, 3 and 1 points above checkpoint a, has the contrast (1 − 1 + 3 + 1) / 4 = 1 point. A resample that draws images 1, 1, 3 and 4 gives (1 + 1 + 3 + 1) / 4 = 1.5; one that draws 2, 2, 4 and 4 gives (−1 − 1 + 1 + 1) / 4 = 0; one that draws 3, 3, 3 and 1 gives (3 + 3 + 3 + 1) / 4 = 2.5. Over many resamples the results spread around 1, and their middle 95 per cent is the interval. An interval that leaves out 0 says that other images of the same kind would rarely turn the difference round; one that contains 0 says that they could. Toy

The interval holds one source of chance only, the images. A second source is the seed of 5.7: two runs that differ only in their seed end with different weights, and that seed spread is not in the interval of a run trained once. A verdict needs it: in the thesis's pre-registered selector study of 5.10, a contrast was declared different when the 95 % interval over the seeds left out zero and the mean difference exceeded a margin fixed in advance, equivalent when the 90 % interval over the seeds lay inside that margin, and inconclusive otherwise. Each contrast of a run here is a single-seed observation, so no verdict of different or equivalent is declared and nothing is adopted. Fact

Against every comparator it claims much less background (13 to 15 points), raises the foreground union IoU by 4 to 5 points and the foreground ARI by 2 to 3, doubles AP100 and returns fewer regions, at the price of a little recall against its start. Under the rule the DINO start ends above the released start by +1.80 [+1.02, +2.61] points of Hungarian IoU. Reading

Run 3, through the head: +0.34 [−0.23, +0.93] against run 1 on the primary endpoint, and run 1's secondary signature is gone. Across the three runs, the rule on the raw tokens changes what the decoder groups, most from the DINO start, while the head version leaves the decoder where its start was. Reading

The linear probe tells another story. Run 1's tokens are more linearly separable than its start's by +1.35 mIoU [0.87, 1.79] while the decoder did not move; run 3 keeps that gain, 1.51 above its start; run 2 reads 4.0 mIoU below run 1 while the decoder ranks the two the other way round. The probe and the decoder reward different properties of the same tokens. Reading

How do the eight checkpoints compare on each endpoint, and which contrasts leave zero out of their interval?

Reading

Choose an endpoint and the checkpoints to show; switch to the contrasts to see each paired difference with its 95 % image-bootstrap interval, drawn in ink when the interval leaves out zero and in grey when it contains zero. Under the chart, one line says what the chosen endpoint measures.

The second seed pair has four runs from pair 2's initial states, seed 907: A repeats run 2 and B the window-term pilot from the DINO start; C repeats run 3 and D run 1 from the released start, all with the run-1 recipe and the rule's values. The amendment plans two evaluations after them, one for the DINO side and one for the SelfPatch side, with decision none, and the probes 9 to 12. With two seeds the thesis can say that a reading repeats in both seeds or in one of two, and no more than that. Fact

5.10 Before the rule: the selector study

Assumes: Part 4. Gives: the question the thesis asked first, what it found, and why it moved on to the rule.

The first question kept SelfPatch's loss and changed only how a patch picks its positives: one shared threshold instead of each patch's own top 4. SelfPatch trains each patch to agree with its 4 most similar neighbours; the thesis replaced that fixed 4 with one similarity threshold shared by a whole crop or a whole training step, hoping that the patches of one object would form islands. Fact

Three rules shared one form, the window neighbours above a threshold: the row rule (SelfPatch's own, the 4th largest of the anchor's 8 similarities), the image rule (one threshold per crop, the median of its similarities) and the batch rule (one threshold per optimiser step). Because they cut the same ranking, the only information a pooled rule adds is a comparison across anchors. Fact

The released-start campaign ran three pairs of row and image runs, seeds 906, 907 and 908. All four pre-registered verdicts of the sealed test reading on image minus row were "equivalent", the 90 % seed-level interval inside a margin of 1 point either side of zero, and the image arm met none of the quality bars. Fact

So far pooling has measured as weaker smoothing: the pooled arms sit where a row rule with k between 2 and 4 would sit, and no term of the loss lowers the agreement of any pair of patches. The report's analyses agreed that a separating term is needed for islands, though it is not enough on its own; this part adds one, a push, beside positives from the whole crop. Fact

5.11 Related ideas

Assumes: 5.1 and 5.6. Gives: where the rule's ideas come from, and what the reading of the literature found.

GLOM proposes islands of identical vectors as the parts of an image, and says that once two representations are sufficiently different there is no further pressure to push them even further apart; the course borrows the picture of islands, never a method. Fact

Run 3's projection head follows the way SimCLR applies its loss and the way DenseCL, Leopart and CrIBo apply their local terms, through a token-wise MLP. Fact

Our rule can be read as a loss that encourages islands of agreeing patch tokens inside one crop and pushes apart the tokens that disagree most. The link to GLOM is that picture and nothing more: the rule has no columns of vectors, no levels and none of GLOM's iterative settling. Reading

Two papers read on 12 October 2026

Two papers were read on 12 October 2026. What their readers found follows, as the lead's summary of their reports gives it. Reading

The Composer (ICLR 2024 submission 297, withdrawn; OpenReview JAfGlmRBTU) is a spiking network of two levels whose neurons synchronise in time: parts and wholes are read out as groups of neurons that fire together. It is trained with a denoising autoencoder for each level, on isolated single parts and wholes, with sixteen hand-set time constants, on four binary synthetic datasets (Ts, Squares, SHOPs and Double MNIST). Its coordination metrics need the true labels of the parts and the wholes, and its binary input gates every firing rate, so figure and ground never have to be separated. Reading

The readers' verdict: the Composer does not solve label-free grouping of photographs, and nothing in it carries over to our trainer. One idea survived, for evaluation only: a silhouette diagnostic of the instances in the frozen decoder's keys, pre-registered and used only to explain, which the owner has not taken up. Reading

Zeng, Song, Zhang, Hu and Yu, Agreement aware and dissimilarity oriented GLOM (ICCV 2025, pages 24351 to 24359) is a column network in GLOM's style that classifies images: SmallNORB, MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. Its contrastive-attention operator is a step of the forward pass and no loss. In every update it splits all the pairs of columns at a level into an attract set and a repel set by a fixed cosine threshold, 0 at the bottom level and −0.2 at the top, and it moves each column toward the softmax-weighted mean of the columns that attract it and away from the columns that repel it. A pooling weighted by dissimilarity cuts its parameters from 72 M to 2 M. Its training is supervised, a supervised contrastive stage and then cross-entropy, and with those labels the paper reports a CIFAR-10 error of 10.90 against Agglomerator's 11.15. Reading

The readers found two defects in the paper's printed mathematics. Its dissimilarity metric reduces to at most 1/d for unit vectors of d numbers, so it cannot reach the published values of 0.37 to 0.54; and its negative term, which uses raw cosines as weights, moves the embeddings toward the negatives. Reading

What this network shares with our rule is the split, gated by a threshold, of all the pairs inside one image into pairs that attract and pairs that repel. Everything else differs: its operator sits inside the forward pass, it trains with labels, it works at the scale of CIFAR and it segments nothing. The readers kept three ideas for later: positives gated by a threshold, which our rule already has through τhi; loosening the positives as training goes on, judged risky; and one step of smoothing the agreement before the decoder, at low priority. Reading

What the literature sweep of 12 October 2026 found

The sweep looked for work after SelfPatch that resembles the rule. It read the citation lists of SelfPatch in Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and OpenCitations, queried the arXiv API, searched OpenReview and read the title listings of CVF, ECCV, NeurIPS, ICLR, PMLR and TMLR, in English only and without Google Scholar. Reading

Within those sources it found no earlier work that trains a ViT backbone with a patch-level InfoNCE whose positives are the anchor's most similar tokens anywhere in the crop, a rank floor plus a crop-wide quantile threshold, and whose negatives are the least similar fifth of the crop, next to DINO's global term, and that reads the result with a frozen spectral decoder on class-agnostic COCO instance masks. Each piece exists somewhere; the combination was not found. This is a statement about the sources searched, and it does not prove that no such work exists. Reading

The nearest works the sweep found: what each shares with our rule, and where it differs. Reading
WorkShares with our ruleDiffers
CoViT (arXiv 2609.01787, September 2026)fine-tunes released DINO ViTs on COCO with a patch InfoNCE inside each imageits positives come from attention masks; its negative is the single most similar patch of another instance, the opposite polarity to our bottom fifth; it drops the global term; it is read by supervised detection
Hidden Positives (CVPR 2023), SmooSeg (NeurIPS 2023) and CAUSEthresholds that attract and repel inside the imagethey train a head on frozen DINO and never the backbone
FLSL (NeurIPS 2023) and CoTAP (TPAMI 2025)positives chosen by similarity beyond a window, with the global term keptsoft weighting or a ranking loss, and no negatives from the crop
CtCAE (NeurIPS 2023)the top k most similar positions as positives and the bottom m least similar as negatives, in an InfoNCEa complex-valued autoencoder on synthetic scenes

Two more works are the precedents for the way we evaluate: DiffNCuts (ECCV 2024) and SimDINO (ICML 2025) each read a short label-free fine-tune, or a changed self-distillation rule, with a frozen spectral decoder on COCO. Reading

The sweep also found evidence against parts of the design, which the thesis should report. Global-Local Self-Distillation (WACV 2023) found local positives mined by similarity harmful when the data are few. ASL (CVPR 2024) argues that a global contrastive term conflicts with patch contrast. VICRegL found a count of positives set by a threshold no better than a fixed count. AdaSim shows that nearest-neighbour positives without negatives can collapse, which is the argument for keeping negatives. Reading

LiFT (ECCV 2024) measured released SelfPatch below DINO on label-free TokenCut, with a COCO20K CorLoc of 52.18 against 53.98. That is the same direction as our decoder's Hungarian matched IoU on the validation panel in 5.9, 15.58 for released SelfPatch against 17.23 for the converted DINO. Reading

No published number is on our scale. The nearest are the Hungarian mIoU of the slot-attention line (7 slots, 256 px), mBO, FG-ARI, class-agnostic AP (bounded by recall for a decoder that returns few regions), CorLoc and semantic mIoU; our background false-positive rate has no published counterpart. Reading

Part 8 lists the summary with the course's other sources, in section 8.3. Fact

Glossary of this page

Anchor
The patch whose partners a rule is choosing. Every patch of a crop is in turn the anchor, and each gets its own positives and negatives.
AP100
The mask average precision of COCO's evaluation with the object categories ignored and up to 100 masks per image. The decoder's masks are ranked by a label-free score; a mask is a hit when its IoU (overlap divided by union) with a true object not yet matched reaches the threshold, and the precision over the levels of recall is averaged over ten thresholds, from an IoU of 50 to 95 per cent.
Attraction
A loss term that only pulls tokens together. SelfPatch's patch loss is attraction only: nothing in it lowers the agreement of any pair of patches.
Bootstrap interval (image-bootstrap interval)
A range for a number measured on a panel of images. Draw the panel's images again at random with replacement, recompute the number, repeat that many times and keep the middle 95 per cent of the results: the interval shows how much the number could move with other images of the same kind. It holds no seed spread.
Contrastive loss
A loss that pulls an anchor towards its positives and pushes it away from its negatives in one formula. For each positive, a softmax over that positive and all the negatives should put most of its weight on the positive; the loss is minus the logarithm of the positive's share. InfoNCE is the contrastive loss of our rule.
Denominator share
In the contrastive loss, the part of the softmax's denominator that one partner holds: wp for the positive and wn for each negative. The shares add up to 1. The negatives' total, 1 − wp, is the weight of the pull, and each negative's share is how hard it pushes.
Direct push
A push considered for the non-local idea and dropped: it adds the overlap of each negative pair itself to the loss, so that every negative pair is pushed apart, however far apart it already is.
Envelope
The file in which a run saves its whole state: the student's and the teacher's weights, the loss's centres, the optimiser's state, the step, the seed and the settings, enough to continue the run or to read it. Our runs write one every 5 epochs, and the last, after epoch 20, is the object of a run.
Epoch
One pass over the training images. In our runs an epoch is 462 optimiser steps of 256 images each.
Exponential moving average (EMA)
A running average that keeps most of its old value at each step and mixes in a little of the new one. DINO's teacher is the exponential moving average of the student's weights.
Heat map
A table of numbers drawn as a grid of cells whose shade shows the size of each number. In Lab N the heat map holds the cosine of every pair of the toy crop.
Hinge
A loss that is zero until a quantity crosses a margin and grows after it. The bounded hinge of the first non-local design pushed a pair apart only while its overlap stayed above a margin; it was dropped.
InfoNCE
The contrastive loss our rule uses. For an anchor and one positive: minus the logarithm of the positive's exponential cosine, over the sum of that and of every negative's exponential cosine, all divided by a temperature first.
Island of agreement
A group of patches whose tokens agree with each other and disagree with the patches around them. GLOM pictures the parts of an image as islands of identical vectors; our rule hopes that each object becomes such an island.
Learning rate
How far one optimiser step moves the weights. Our runs give the heads a learning rate that peaks at 1e-4 and the backbone one that peaks at 1e-5.
Negative
A patch that a rule chooses for an anchor to disagree with. Under our rule: a patch of the same crop at or below the crop's low threshold, never one of the anchor's positives, at most 48 per anchor.
Optimiser step
One update of every weight of the network, from the gradients of one batch of images. Our runs take 9,240 of them.
Overlap
In the pushes that were considered first, oij: the sum over the prototypes of the student's probability for anchor i times the teacher's target probability for patch j. It is 0 when the two share no prototype and 1 only when both put everything on the same one.
Paired contrast
The mean, over the same images, of one checkpoint's value minus another's on each image. Each image is compared with itself, so what makes an image easy or hard for both checkpoints cancels in its difference.
Pilot
An earlier run of the project: DINO trained with SelfPatch's own window term under recipe LC0 for 20 epochs. It is run 2's comparator from the same DINO start.
Positive
A patch that a rule chooses for an anchor to agree with. Under our rule: one of the anchor's k most similar patches, or any patch of the crop at or above the crop's high threshold, at most 24 per anchor.
Prototype
One of the learned directions that a projection head compares a token with. DINO's head has 65,536 prototypes and SelfPatch's patch head 4,096; the toy of Lab N has 8.
Quantile
The value below which a given share of a sorted list falls. The 0.20 quantile of a crop's cosines has a fifth of them at or below it; between two sorted values, linear interpolation takes the point in between.
Seed
The number from which a run draws everything random: in our runs the order of the images in each epoch, the crops of every image, the random numbers of every step and, from the DINO start, the first weights of the fresh heads. Two runs that differ only in their seed differ by chance alone. Our first runs used seed 906; the second seed pair uses 907.
Stop-gradient
Treating a quantity as a fixed number when the loss is differentiated, so that no gradient flows into it. The teacher's tokens are behind a stop-gradient; only the student's tokens move by the loss.
Telemetry (progress line)
The numbers a trainer writes about itself while it runs: one line per optimiser step with the losses, the learning rates and the rule's statistics, read afterwards to see how training went.
Temperature
A number that the cosines are divided by before a softmax. A small temperature sharpens the softmax towards its largest entry; our rule's term uses 0.2.
Toy step
One training step of a lab's toy. The gradient moves the toy's tokens directly, each is scaled back to length 1, and in Lab N the teacher's tokens move a tenth of the way towards the student's. A real step moves the network's weights instead.
Twin (LC0 twin)
One of the campaign's two runs of pair 1 under recipe LC0, trained with SelfPatch's own patch term from run 1's start, with the same seed, images, order and crops as run 1: the row twin with SelfPatch's rule, the image twin with the pooled rule.
Verdict (different, equivalent)
The conclusion that a pre-registered rule draws from an interval over several seeds: different when the 95 % interval leaves out zero and the mean difference exceeds a margin fixed in advance, equivalent when the 90 % interval lies inside that margin, and inconclusive otherwise. One seed gives no interval over seeds, so the readings of a single run declare none.
Warm-up
The first epochs of training, during which the learning rate rises in a straight line from 0 to its peak, so that the first steps stay small.
Weight decay
A small pull of every decayed weight towards 0 at each step, which AdamW applies apart from the gradient. Our runs raise it from 0.04 to 0.4.
Within-object cosine
In Lab N, the mean cosine between two patches of the same object: cat with cat, ball with ball, fence with fence. The grass, the background, is counted on its own. When it rises while the cosine between patches of different kinds falls, islands are forming.
